issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not reassess evidence and displace concurrent factual findings unless the findings suffer from material illegality, impropriety, or perversity.
material_facts: The Rent Controller ordered eviction on findings that the tenant had ceased occupying the premises without reasonable cause and had shifted with his family to another reasonably sufficient house.
The Appellate Authority reassessed the evidence and affirmed the eviction order.
In revision, the High Court re-evaluated the evidence and set aside the concurrent findings without establishing that they were perverse or unsupported by evidence.

The Supreme Court found that the lower authorities had thoroughly considered the evidence, while the High Court relied on occasional visits by family members living elsewhere and disregarded evidence that the resident family had shifted to the other house.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in disturbing the concurrent findings; its judgment was set aside and the eviction orders were restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(6) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 gives the High Court revisional power to examine the legality or propriety of an order, a power wider than revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure but not equivalent to an appeal. Unlike an appeal, revision does not ordinarily permit reassessment of evidence. Concurrent findings properly based on evidence should not be disturbed unless they are wholly perverse or erroneous, manifestly unjust, or affected by material illegality or impropriety. The Court relied on State of Kerala v. K.M. Charia Abdullah & Co. (1965), Hari Shankar v. Rao Girdhari Lal Chowdhury (1962), and Neta Ram v. Jivan Lal (1963).

rule.if: rent_control_revision and concurrent_factual_findings and findings_supported_by_evidence and not material_perversity_or_illegality and revisional_court_reweighed_evidence

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding is a revision concerning an order made in a rent-control matter.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The first-instance authority and the appellate authority reached the same factual conclusions.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: The lower authorities based their factual conclusions on evidence they examined.
predicates.material_perversity_or_illegality: The findings are affected by material perversity or illegality.
predicates.revisional_court_reweighed_evidence: The revisional court reassessed the evidence to reach a different factual conclusion.

issues.definition: When a rent-control revision concerns concurrent factual findings supported by evidence and unaffected by material perversity or illegality, a revisional court's reassessment of the evidence does not justify disturbing those findings.

issues.legal_issue: Eviction may be sustained where the evidence establishes that a tenant ceased occupying the premises without reasonable cause and shifted with the resident family to reasonably sufficient alternative accommodation.
material_facts: The Rent Controller found that the tenant had ceased occupying the premises for more than four months without reasonable cause.
The Rent Controller found that the tenant had acquired another house in his wife's name and that the tenant, his wife, and the family members living with them had shifted there.
The two houses had almost the same capacity, and the evidence showed that the resident family consisted of six members who had shifted to the acquired house.
The High Court treated family members who lived or worked elsewhere but visited occasionally as part of the household and concluded that the other house was insufficient.
issues.conclusion: The findings supporting eviction under the statutory grounds were restored, and the eviction order was reinstated.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 13(2)(v) and 13(3)(a)(iv) of the Haryana Urban (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1973 provide grounds of eviction for a tenant's cessation of occupation without reasonable cause and for acquisition or possession of reasonably sufficient alternative accommodation, respectively. The Court accepted the concurrent findings that the tenant had ceased occupying the premises and that the house acquired in his wife's name was reasonably sufficient for the family actually residing with him; occasional visits by other family members did not establish that they lived in either house.

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant from rented premises.
predicates.tenant_ceased_occupying_without_reasonab: The tenant stopped occupying the rented premises for the relevant continuous period without a reasonable cause.
predicates.resident_family_shifted_to_alternative_h: The tenant and the family members living with the tenant moved to another home available to the tenant.
predicates.alternative_home_reasonably_sufficient: The other home was reasonably sufficient for the tenant and the family members actually residing with the tenant.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding establishes that the tenant stopped occupying the rented premises without reasonable cause and the resident family moved to reasonably sufficient alternative accommodation, eviction on those grounds is sustainable.
